title: Secondhand: A Conversation About What Was Said

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: I need to tell you what happened in Professor Akhmetov's seminar on Wednesday. It was interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Go on. I missed it — I had a dentist appointment.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: He said that too many students were writing essays that summarised sources without engaging with them. He insisted that the point of academic writing wasn't to report what others had said but to think about what it meant.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: He showed us two paragraphs. In the first one, the student had written "Smith argues that X. Jones argues that Y. Brown argues that Z." He said it read like a list, not an argument.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: The second one engaged with the sources. It said something like "Smith argues that X, but this claim is undermined by Jones's evidence that Y." He told us to aim for that.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That makes sense. Did anyone ask questions?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Amir asked whether reported speech rules applied in academic writing too — whether you had to shift tenses when you cited sources.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: He explained that in academic writing, the convention was different from grammar exercises. He said that when you cited someone's work, you usually used the present tense — "Smith argues" not "Smith argued" — unless the work was clearly outdated.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That's useful. Did he say anything about reporting verbs specifically?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: He warned us that choosing the wrong reporting verb could change the meaning of what we were trying to convey. He gave the example of "acknowledge" vs "admit." He said they were similar but that "admit" carries a stronger sense that something went wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I wish I'd been there. Did he set any work?

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: He asked us to revise one paragraph from our last essay and replace all the "says/said" with more precise reporting verbs. He recommended choosing three or four from the list he'd given us.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I can do that for mine too. Thanks — you've reported it much better than most people would have.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: I was paying attention specifically because I knew you'd ask.

questions.text: "He said that too many students WERE writing essays without engaging." — Past Continuous because:
opts: It describes an ongoing pattern at that time, not a single event
questions.correct: It describes an ongoing pattern at that time, not a single event
questions.hint: PC in reported speech = PC (backshift not needed here as it was Past Continuous → Past Continuous). The "pattern" interpretation suits PC. ✅

questions.text: "Amir asked WHETHER reported speech rules applied in academic writing." — "whether" because:
opts: It's a yes/no question converted to reported form
questions.correct: It's a yes/no question converted to reported form
questions.hint: "whether" (or "if") introduces yes/no questions in reported speech. "Do they apply?" → asked WHETHER they applied. ✅

questions.text: "He explained THAT in academic writing, the convention WAS different." — why "was" not "is"?
opts: Tense backshift: present → past in reported speech
questions.correct: Tense backshift: present → past in reported speech
questions.hint: Present Simple → Past Simple in reported speech. "is different" → "was different." ✅ (Or "is" if treating as still-true fact.)
